::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**From the [Swarm Systems Lab](https://www.swarmsystemslab.eu/publications/guiding-vector-fields-for-the-distributed-motion-coordination-of-mobile),** University of Granada. To try the results by hand, open the
[playground](playground.html).

**What this page does.** It takes the paper *Guiding vector fields for the distributed motion coordination of mobile
robots* (its LaTeX source, `multi_jrn_main.tex`) and writes it out for one of the paper's own examples: 21 robots on
three concentric paths, seven on each, that keep equal spacings in their path parameters (the paper's third
simulation). It goes step by step: one robot and its virtual coordinate (Section II-C of the paper), the coordination
component that couples the robots (Section III), why it works from any start (Theorem 1), surfaces instead of paths
(Section IV, Theorem 2), collisions (Section V), and fixed-wing aircraft at constant speed (Section VI, Theorem 3). It
ends with the program each robot runs, and with the paper's four simulations and two flights run again.

**Source and status.** The results are the paper's, and this page does not re-prove them. It adds a few things of its
own, each marked where it appears: one reading of the Lyapunov derivative (@sec-lyap), the speed of the coordination
on a path (@sec-rate), and two remarks on the proofs (@sec-proofs). Every number on the page is computed by `core.py` when the page is rendered. The interactive figures run
`assets/core.js`, and `make check` proves that the two agree.
:::

# The problem

$N$ robots move in $\mathbb R^n$ ($n = 2$ in the example, $n = 3$ for the aircraft). Robot $i$ is a single
integrator, $\dot x^{[i]} = u^{[i]}$, until @sec-air replaces it with a fixed-wing aircraft.

**Its path.** Robot $i$ has its own path, given by a parametrisation $x = f^{[i]}(w)$, $w \in \mathbb R$. Different
robots may have different paths. A path may cross itself, need not be closed, and need not be given by an implicit
equation. Only $f^{[i]}$ and its first two derivatives are needed, and they must be bounded (Assumption 2).

**What it measures.** Its own position $x^{[i]}$ (a GPS on the aircraft of the paper). Nothing about the other
robots' positions, except in @sec-safe, where it measures the positions of the robots close to it.

**What is shared.** Each robot keeps one number of its own, the *virtual coordinate* $w^{[i]}$: where it is on its
path, in the units of the parameter. It sends that number to its neighbours in an undirected graph, and receives
theirs (Remark 2). For every neighbour $j$ it knows a desired difference $\Delta^{[i,j]} = -\Delta^{[j,i]}$.

**The task** (Problem 1). From any start, every robot converges to its path, $\|\Phi^{[i]}\| \to 0$, and every edge
reaches its desired difference, $w^{[i]} - w^{[j]} - \Delta^{[i,j]} \to 0$.

**Why it is hard.** Nothing tells the robots where to be at what time: there is no clock to follow, no leader, and
no common frame on the path. Each robot only knows its own path and a few numbers from its neighbours, and the
team must agree on its spacing while it moves. The paper does this with one extra coordinate per robot, and the
field it builds has no point where it vanishes, so no start is a trap.

**The example.** The paper's third simulation (its Fig. 5). Robots 1 to 7 are on the circle of radius $a = 10$,
robots 8 to 14 on the ellipse with half-axes $a = 10$ and $b = 5$, and robots 15 to 21 on the circle of radius
$b = 5$:

$$
f^{[i]}(w) = \begin{pmatrix} 10\cos w \\ 10 \sin w \end{pmatrix},\qquad
f^{[i]}(w) = \begin{pmatrix} 10\cos w \\ 5 \sin w \end{pmatrix},\qquad
f^{[i]}(w) = \begin{pmatrix} 5\cos w \\ 5 \sin w \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The graph is the cycle $1 - 2 - \dots - 21 - 1$: each robot talks to two others. The spacing is equal in the path
parameter: the reference is $w^{[i]*} = (i-1)\,2\pi/21$, so $\Delta^{[i,i+1]} = -2\pi/21$ for the first 20 edges
and $\Delta^{[21,1]} = 20 \cdot 2\pi/21$ for the edge that closes the cycle. The gains are $k_1 = k_2 = 1$ and
$k_c = 100$.

# Step 1: one robot and its virtual coordinate {#sec-one}

## A path one dimension up

A path in $\mathbb R^n$ is the zero set of $n$ functions once $w$ is a coordinate of its own (Section II-C of the
paper). With the *generalised coordinate* $\xi = (x_1, \dots, x_n, w) \in \mathbb R^{n+1}$ and

$$
\phi_j(\xi) = x_j - f_j(w), \qquad j = 1, \dots, n,
$$

the set where all the $\phi_j$ vanish is the graph of the path, $\{(f(w), w)\}$, a curve in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ that
never crosses itself, even when $f$ does: two points of it with the same $x$ have different $w$. The paper's field
(1) is a wedge product of the gradients $\nabla\phi_j$, which runs along that curve, minus a term that pulls towards
it:

$$
\chi(\xi) = \wedge\left(\nabla\phi_1, \dots, \nabla\phi_n\right) - \sum_{j=1}^n k_j\,\phi_j\,\nabla\phi_j .
$$

Written out, it is (3):

$$
\chi = \begin{pmatrix} (-1)^n f_1'(w) - k_1\phi_1 \\ \vdots \\ (-1)^n f_n'(w) - k_n\phi_n \\
(-1)^n + \sum_{l} k_l\,\phi_l\, f_l'(w) \end{pmatrix}.
$$

The first $n$ entries move the robot, and the last one moves $w$. It never vanishes (this line is ours): if the first
$n$ entries are zero, then $k_j\phi_j = (-1)^n f'_j$, and the last entry is $(-1)^n\left(1 + \|f'\|^2\right) \neq 0$.
This is the property of the singularity-free field that the paper builds on (its references [yao2021singularity],
[yao2020mobile]).

## The field for the example

For robot 8, on the ellipse ($n = 2$, so $(-1)^n = 1$), with $k_1 = k_2 = 1$:

$$
\chi^{[8]} = \begin{pmatrix} -10\sin w - \phi_1 \\ 5\cos w - \phi_2 \\ 1 - 10\,\phi_1 \sin w + 5\,\phi_2 \cos w \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \phi_1 = x_1 - 10\cos w,\quad \phi_2 = x_2 - 5\sin w .
$$

On the path ($\phi = 0$) the robot moves at $f'(w)$ and its virtual coordinate at $\dot w = 1$: the ellipse is run
counterclockwise. Off the path, $w$ is in a closed loop with the robot: it moves ahead faster when the robot is
ahead of its guiding point $f(w)$, and slows down or goes back when the robot is behind (the paper's remark on the
"carrot"). The figure shows a robot alone, with its guiding point.

```{=html}
<div id="ex-one" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wOne("ex-one")</script>
```

# Step 2: a coordination component {#sec-coord}

## The coordination function

On the path, every robot's virtual coordinate runs at the same rate, $\dot w = (-1)^n$. So differences of $w$ are
conserved, and they are the natural thing to coordinate. The paper adds one term to the last entry of the field,
(4) and (5),

$$
\chi^{[i]} = \chi^{[i]}_{\mathrm{pf}} + k_c \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ c^{[i]} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
c^{[i]} = -\sum_{j \in \mathcal N_i} \left( w^{[i]} - w^{[j]} - \Delta^{[i,j]} \right),
$$

the consensus law (7). In stacked form $c = -L(w - w^*)$, with $L$ the Laplacian of the graph and $w^*$ any
reference with $\Delta^{[i,j]} = w^{[i]*} - w^{[j]*}$ (8). The robots never need $w^*$ itself, only the differences
with their neighbours.

The coordination term acts only on $w$. It does not push the robot: it moves the robot's guiding point along the path,
forward when the robot is behind its neighbours in $w$, back when it is ahead, and the path-following part then
brings the robot to its guiding point.

## For the example

Robot 8 is between robot 7 (on the large circle) and robot 9 (on the ellipse):

$$
c^{[8]} = -\left(w^{[8]} - w^{[7]} - \tfrac{2\pi}{21}\right) - \left(w^{[8]} - w^{[9]} + \tfrac{2\pi}{21}\right),
\qquad \dot w^{[8]} = 1 - 10\,\phi_1 \sin w^{[8]} + 5\,\phi_2 \cos w^{[8]} + 100\, c^{[8]} .
$$

It sends one number, $w^{[8]}$, to robots 7 and 9, and receives theirs. In steady motion the team keeps
$w^{[i+1]} = w^{[i]} + 2\pi/21$. Robots on different paths then sit at the same angle parameter but at different
places, so the team makes a pattern that changes shape as it turns: the three groups bunch and spread out as they pass
the axes of the ellipse (the paper's "varying formation shapes").

```{=html}
<div id="ex-team" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wTeam("ex-team")</script>
```

# Step 3: why it works, from any start (Theorem 1) {#sec-thm1}

## The composite error

Theorem 1 of the paper: under Assumptions 1 (the graph is undirected and connected) and 2 (bounded $f'$ and $f''$),
with constant $\Delta$, the field (5) with (7) solves Problem 1 *globally*: the composite error

$$
e = \begin{pmatrix} \Phi \\ D^\top \tilde w \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \tilde w = w - w^*,
$$

goes to zero from any start. $\Phi$ stacks the path-following errors of all robots, and $D^\top\tilde w$ the
coordination errors of all edges ($D$ is an incidence matrix, $L = DD^\top$). The proof (Appendix A) uses

$$
V = \tfrac12\left(\Phi^\top K \Phi + k_c\,\tilde w^\top L\,\tilde w\right)
= \tfrac12\sum_i \Phi^{[i]\top} K^{[i]} \Phi^{[i]} + \tfrac{k_c}{2}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal E}\left(w^{[i]} - w^{[j]} - \Delta^{[i,j]}\right)^2
$$

(41), and finds (45)

$$
\dot V = -\|K\Phi\|^2 - \left\|\mathfrak F^\top K\Phi - k_c L\tilde w\right\|^2 \le 0,
$$

with $\mathfrak F = \operatorname{diag}(f^{[1]\prime}, \dots, f^{[N]\prime})$.

## What $\dot V$ says {#sec-lyap}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# (45) against a finite difference of V along the flow, at a few instants of the example
vd_rows = []
for kk in (0, 5, 50, 300):
    X = run21[kk]
    V0, Vd = lyapunov(T21, X)
    h = 1e-7
    X1, _ = step(T21, X, h)
    V1, _ = lyapunov(T21, X1)
    vd_rows.append((t21[kk], V0, Vd, (V1 - V0) / h))
vd_gap = max(abs(a[2] - a[3]) / max(1.0, abs(a[2])) for a in vd_rows)
```

The $i$-th entry of $\mathfrak F^\top K\Phi - k_c L\tilde w$ is $f^{[i]\prime\top}K^{[i]}\Phi^{[i]} + k_c c^{[i]}$,
and by (38) that is $\dot w^{[i]} - (-1)^n$. So (this reading is ours)

$$
\dot V = -\|K\Phi\|^2 - \sum_i \left(\dot w^{[i]} - (-1)^n\right)^2 .
$$

$V$ falls as long as some robot is off its path, or some robot's virtual coordinate runs at another rate than the
nominal one. A team whose robots are on their paths and whose $w$'s all run at the nominal rate has $\dot V = 0$, and
then, since every $\dot w^{[i]}$ equals $(-1)^n$ and $c^{[i]} = 0$ for all $i$, every edge is at its desired
difference. This is how `core.py` computes $\dot V$. Against a finite difference of $V$ along the example's run, the
largest relative gap is `{python} e1(vd_gap)`:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = ["| time | $V$ | $\\dot V$ from (45) | $\\dot V$, finite difference |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
rows += [f"| {t:.1f} s | {v:.4g} | {a:.6g} | {b:.6g} |" for t, v, a, b in vd_rows]
print("\n".join(rows))
```

```{=html}
<div id="ex-lyap" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wLyap("ex-lyap")</script>
```

## Two remarks on the proofs {#sec-proofs}

Both are ours, and neither changes a result.

- **Theorem 1 cites LaSalle's invariance principle** (Khalil, Theorem 4.4). That theorem asks for an autonomous
  system with a compact positively invariant set. The state is $\xi$, which contains every $w^{[i]}$, and the $w$'s grow
  without bound (they run at $(-1)^n$), so no sublevel set of $V$ is compact in $\xi$. The error dynamics (40) do
  not close in $e$ either: they depend on $w$ through $\mathfrak F$. The proof of Theorem 2 (Appendix B) uses
  Barbalat's lemma instead, with Assumption 3, and that argument covers the path case as it stands (one parameter
  instead of two). So Theorem 1 holds; its proof is the one of Theorem 2.
- **Connectivity (Assumption 1) is not what makes the edges converge.** The proof shows $D^\top\tilde w \to 0$,
  which is the coordination error of every edge, for any graph. What connectivity adds is that the edges then fix
  every pair of robots. On a graph cut in two, each part coordinates, and the offset between the parts is whatever
  the transient left. The figure above has the cut; the playground's census runs it on random teams.

## How fast {#sec-rate}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# the slow mode of the coordination on a circle: three robots on a circle of radius a, one of them pushed along
def rate_measured(a, kc, k):
    S = shape("circle", a=a)
    T = team([S] * 3, cycle(3), even_ref(3, 2 * math.pi), [[k, k]] * 3, [kc])
    X = [list(shape_eval(S, [w[0]])[0]) + [w[0]] for w in T["ws_ref"]]
    X[0][2] += 0.2
    X[0][0], X[0][1] = shape_eval(S, [X[0][2]])[0]
    ec = []
    dt = 1e-3
    for s in range(30000):
        X, _ = step(T, X, dt)
        if s % 1000 == 999:
            ec.append(errors(T, X)[1])
    return -math.log(ec[25] / ec[10]) / 15
def rate_linear(a, kc, k, lam=3.0):
    M = np.array([[-k * (1 + a * a), -1, kc * a * lam], [1, -k, 0], [k * a, 0, -kc * lam]])
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(M)
    return float(-max(ev.real))
RATE_CASES = [(2.0, 1.0, 1.0), (5.0, 1.0, 1.0), (10.0, 0.5, 1.0), (5.0, 1.0, 3.0), (5.0, 20.0, 1.0)]
rate_rows = cached("rates", lambda: [(a, kc, k, rate_linear(a, kc, k), rate_measured(a, kc, k)) for a, kc, k in RATE_CASES])
lam2_50 = 2 * (1 - math.cos(2 * math.pi / 50))
fp_eight = [math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in shape_eval(shape("eight3d"), [w])[1][0])) for w in np.linspace(0, 2 * math.pi, 400)]
fp2_mean = float(np.mean(np.array(fp_eight) ** 2))
tau_eight = {kc: (1 + fp2_mean) / (kc * lam2_50 * 2) for kc in (1.0, 300.0)}
```

Theorem 1 says nothing about how fast. A short linearisation shows what sets the speed (ours, checked against the
simulation). Take robots on a circle of radius $a$, with $K = kI$, and write each $\Phi$ in the frame of the path:
$\Phi_t$ along it, $\Phi_n$ across it. The frame turns with $w$, which couples the two. For one mode of the Laplacian,
with eigenvalue $\lambda$, near the path:

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\begin{pmatrix} \Phi_t \\ \Phi_n \\ \tilde w \end{pmatrix} =
\begin{pmatrix} -k(1+a^2) & -1 & k_c\, a\, \lambda \\ 1 & -k & 0 \\ k\,a & 0 & -k_c\lambda \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \Phi_t \\ \Phi_n \\ \tilde w \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Its slowest eigenvalue sets the rate of the coordination. The table compares it with the rate measured on three
robots on the circle ($\lambda = 3$), one of them pushed ahead by $0.2$ in $w$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = ["| radius $a$ | $k_c$ | $k$ | slowest rate, linearisation | rate measured, simulation |", "|---|---|---|---|---|"]
rows += [f"| {a:g} | {kc:g} | {k:g} | {f3(r1)} | {f3(r2)} |" for a, kc, k, r1, r2 in rate_rows]
print("\n".join(rows))
```

When $k_c\lambda$ is small next to $k(1+a^2)$, the slowest rate is close to
$k_c\lambda\,(1+k^2)\,/\,\left(k^2(1+a^2)\right)$: the coordination slows down as $1/\|f'\|^2$. The robot must
travel $\|f'\|$ in space for every unit of $w$ it corrects, and the path-following term, which grows as $\|f'\|^2$,
holds it to its guiding point. This explains a choice in the paper. On the figure eight of its first simulation
$\|f'\|$ goes up to `{python} f1(max(fp_eight))`, and the slowest mode of the cycle of 50 robots has
$\lambda_2$ = `{python} f3(lam2_50)`. With the mean of $\|f'\|^2$ along the eight in the estimate above, the time
constant of that mode would be about `{python} f1(tau_eight[1.0] / 3600)` hours with $k_c = 1$. The paper takes
$k_c = 300$, "large to accelerate the motion coordination", and the estimate drops to about
`{python} f1(tau_eight[300.0])` s, which is the scale of its Fig. 3 **[numerical]**.

# Step 4: surfaces (Theorem 2) {#sec-surf}

## Two virtual coordinates and an extra vector

A surface needs two parameters, $x = f^{[i]}(w_1, w_2)$, and each robot keeps two virtual coordinates. The
generalised coordinate is $\xi = (x, w_1, w_2) \in \mathbb R^{n+2}$, and the $n$ gradients $\nabla\phi_j$ are not
enough for a wedge product in $n + 2$ dimensions. The paper adds an *extra vector* $v$ (14), and with
$v = (0, \dots, 0, v_{n+1}, v_{n+2})$ the field is (15):

$$
\chi_{\mathrm{sf}} = (-1)^n \begin{pmatrix} v_{n+2}\,\partial_{w_1} f - v_{n+1}\,\partial_{w_2} f \\ v_{n+2} \\ -v_{n+1} \end{pmatrix}
+ \begin{pmatrix} -K\Phi \\ \partial_{w_1} f^\top K\Phi \\ \partial_{w_2} f^\top K\Phi \end{pmatrix}.
$$

On a surface a robot has a direction to choose, and $v$ chooses it. Theorem 2 takes
$v = (-1)^{n+1}(0, \dots, 0, \dot w_2^*, -\dot w_1^*)$. With that choice the field reads (this rewriting is ours)

$$
\chi_{\mathrm{sf}} = \begin{pmatrix} \partial_{w_1} f\,\dot w_1^* + \partial_{w_2} f\,\dot w_2^* - K\Phi \\ \dot w_1^* + \partial_{w_1} f^\top K\Phi \\ \dot w_2^* + \partial_{w_2} f^\top K\Phi \end{pmatrix},
$$

which is the path field of Step 1 with $(-1)^n$ replaced by the desired parametric speeds $\dot w^*$: on the surface
the robot moves at $\partial_{w_1} f\,\dot w_1^* + \partial_{w_2} f\,\dot w_2^*$, and its virtual coordinates at
$\dot w^*$. Each parameter gets its own consensus term (16), (19), with gains $k_{c1}, k_{c2}$, and each robot sends
two numbers.

Theorem 2: under Assumptions 1 and 3 (bounded first and second derivatives), with constant $\Delta_1$, $\Delta_2$, the
field solves Problem 2 globally: every robot converges to its surface, every edge to its two desired differences, and
every robot's virtual coordinates to the speeds $\dot w^*$. The Lyapunov function is (55), the same as above with one
consensus term per parameter, and the reading of @sec-lyap carries over:
$\dot V = -\|K\Phi\|^2 - \sum_{i,p}\left(\dot w_p^{[i]} - \dot w^*_p\right)^2$.

## The sphere of Example 2

```{python}
#| echo: false
SPH = {}
for ws in ([0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]):
    T = example2_team(ws)
    run = cached(f"sphere{ws[0]}", lambda T=T: simulate(T, [[0.5, 1.2, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0], [-1.0, -1.0, 0.8, 0.3, 0.2]], 1e-3, 20000, 50))
    SPH[ws[0]] = (T, run)
sph_err = {k: errors(T, run[-1]) for k, (T, run) in SPH.items()}
```

The paper's Example 2 puts two robots on the unit sphere (12),

$$
f = (\cos w_1 \cos w_2,\ \cos w_1\sin w_2,\ \sin w_1),
$$

with $\Delta^{[1,2]}_1 = \Delta^{[1,2]}_2 = -\pi$, in two scenarios: $\dot w^* = (0, 1)$ and $\dot w^* = (1, 1)$ (its
Fig. 1). Here $n = 3$, so $v = (0, 0, 0, \dot w_2^*, -\dot w_1^*)$. Shifting both parameters by $\pi$ keeps $\cos w_1 \cos w_2$ and $\cos w_1 \sin w_2$ and changes the sign of
$\sin w_1$: robot 2 sits at robot 1's mirror image across the equator. In the first scenario both run along parallels, one north and one south;
in the second their paths wind over the sphere. After 20 s of the run below, the largest path error is
`{python} e1(max(sph_err[0.0][0], sph_err[1.0][0]))` and the coordination error `{python} e1(max(sph_err[0.0][1], sph_err[1.0][1]))`.

# Step 5: collisions (Section V) {#sec-safe}

```{python}
#| echo: false
def crossing_team(N=8, span=2 * math.pi):
    return team([shape("eight3d")] * N, cycle(N), even_ref(N, span), [[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]] * N, [5.0])
def crossing_run(mode, span=2 * math.pi, R=3.0, alpha=0.5, Rs=6.0, tend=30.0, dt=5e-4):
    T = crossing_team(8, span)
    X = [list(shape_eval(T["S"][0], [w[0] + 0.5])[0]) + [w[0] + 0.5] for w in T["ws_ref"]]
    sf = None if mode is None else {"R": R, "alpha": alpha, "mode": mode, "Rs": Rs}
    md, ecs = [], []
    for s in range(int(tend / dt)):
        X, _ = step(T, X, dt, sf)
        if s % 20 == 0:
            md.append(mindist(X, 3))
            ecs.append(errors(T, X)[1])
    return {"md": md, "ec": ecs, "X": X}
CROSS = cached("cross", lambda: {m: crossing_run(m) for m in (None, "range")})
CROSS_HALF = cached("cross_half", lambda: crossing_run(None, math.pi))
```

The coordination is in parameter space. Two robots with different $w$ can still be at the same place: on a path that
crosses itself, or on two paths that cross. The paper's first simulation spreads its 50 robots over *half* of the
figure eight, $w^{[i]*} = (i-1)\,T/(2N)$, and this is why: the eight crosses itself at $w = 0$ and $w = \pi$, so two
robots half a period apart reach the crossing at the same time. Spread eight robots over the whole period and they
meet there twice a lap: the closest two come within `{python} f3(min(CROSS[None]["md"]))` of each other. Over half
the period they never come closer than `{python} f2(min(CROSS_HALF["md"]))`.

Section V of the paper adds a *safety barrier certificate* (Wang, Ames, Egerstedt 2017). With a safety distance $R$,
$h_{ij} = \|P(\xi^{[i]} - \xi^{[j]})\|^2 - R^2$ (where $P$ keeps the position and drops $w$) and $B_{ij} = 1/h_{ij}$
(23), each robot solves its own small quadratic program (QP2): the command closest to its field $\chi^{[i]}$ with

$$
(\xi^{[j]} - \xi^{[i]})^\top P^\top \check\chi^{[i]} \le \tfrac{\alpha}{4}\, h_{ij}^3 \qquad \text{for } j \in \mathcal D_i .
$$

The constraint only touches the position part, so $w$ runs as before, and only robot $i$'s own command is changed. It
needs the positions of the robots near it, measured, not communicated. Here the page solves (QP2) with Hildreth's
method, 40 sweeps per tick.

The set $\mathcal D_i$ holds the robots within a sensing distance $R_s > R$ of robot $i$, so the barrier starts to
act before two robots reach the safety distance (here $R_s = 2R$). On the eight robots above, with $R = 3$ and
$\alpha = 0.5$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = ["| (QP2) | closest two robots over 30 s | largest coordination error, last 10 s |", "|---|---|---|"]
names = {None: "off", "range": "on, $R_s = 6$"}
for m in (None, "range"):
    c = CROSS[m]
    rows.append(f"| {names[m]} | {f3(min(c['md']))} | {f3(max(c['ec'][-1000:]))} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

The certificate keeps the robots apart. The price is the coordination: the robots on this spacing must dodge each other
twice a lap, forever, so the coordination error never settles. The paper's remark after (QP2) asks for exactly
this: design the paths and the $\Delta$'s so that robots at their desired spacing are further apart than $R$. The
certificate then only acts in the transient.

# Step 6: fixed-wing aircraft (Theorem 3) {#sec-air}

## The model and the partial normalisation

```{python}
#| echo: false
fl_start = [{"x": [-150.0, 60.0, 10.0], "th": 0.3, "w": [0.0]}, {"x": [100.0, -40.0, -5.0], "th": 2.0, "w": [100.0]}]
def flight_summary(A, st0, tend, wind=(0.0, 0.0), dt=0.1):
    fl = fly(A, st0, dt, int(tend / dt), 10, wind)
    T = A["T"]
    rows = []
    for s in fl:
        X = [[q["x"][l] + A["bias"][i][l] for l in range(3)] + q["w"] for i, q in enumerate(s["st"])]
        ep, ec = errors(T, X)
        be = T["S"][0].get("beta") or [1.0] * T["S"][0]["k"]
        ecp = max(abs((X[0][3 + p] - X[1][3 + p]) - (T["ws_ref"][0][p] - T["ws_ref"][1][p])) * be[p] for p in range(T["S"][0]["k"]))
        rows.append((s["t"], ep, ec, math.dist(s["st"][0]["x"], s["st"][1]["x"]),
                     max(abs(x) for x in s.get("thd", [0.0])), max(s.get("sat", [0.0])), ecp))
    return np.array(rows), fl
FL1 = cached("fl1", lambda: flight_summary(flight1(), fl_start, 600.0))
FL1d = cached("fl1d", lambda: flight_summary(flight1(delta=math.pi / 2), fl_start, 1200.0))
fl2_start = [{"x": [90.0, 10.0, 48.0], "th": 1.5, "w": [0.0, 0.0]}, {"x": [-20.0, 99.0, 55.0], "th": 3.0, "w": [300.0, 100.0]}]
FL2 = cached("fl2", lambda: flight_summary(flight2(), fl2_start, 900.0))
late = lambda R, t0: R[R[:, 0] >= t0]
d_thd = max(late(FL1[0], 300)[:, 4])
sat_all = float(np.mean(FL1[0][1:, 5] > 0))
sat_late = float(np.mean(late(FL1[0], 300)[:, 5] > 0))
```

The paper's aircraft is a Dubins-car-like model (28): it flies at a constant speed $v$, turns at a rate
$u_\theta$, and climbs at a rate $u_z$:

$$
\dot p_1 = v\cos\theta, \quad \dot p_2 = v\sin\theta, \quad \dot p_3 = u_z, \quad \dot\theta = u_\theta .
$$

It cannot follow $\chi$ as a velocity: it cannot slow down, and it cannot stop. So the field is *partially
normalised*: scaled so that its horizontal part has the length $v$. The aircraft turns towards the horizontal part,
and copies the rest (29):

$$
u_z = \frac{v\,\chi_3}{\sqrt{\chi_1^2 + \chi_2^2}}, \qquad \dot w_p = \frac{v\,\chi_{3+p}}{\sqrt{\chi_1^2 + \chi_2^2}} .
$$

## The heading law, and saturation

With $\hat\chi_p$ the direction of the horizontal part, $h = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$, $E$ the rotation by $90°$, and
$\sigma$ the angle from $\hat\chi_p$ to $h$ (so $h^\top E\hat\chi_p = \sin\sigma$), the turn rate is (31)

$$
u_\theta = \operatorname{Sat}_a^b\!\left(\dot\theta_d - k_\theta\, h^\top E\, \hat\chi_p\right), \qquad
\dot\theta_d = -\frac{\hat\chi_p^\top E\,\dot\chi_p}{\|\chi_p\|} ,
$$

where $\dot\theta_d$ (32) is the rate at which the field's direction turns along the aircraft's motion. It needs the
derivative of the field, $\dot\chi = J\dot\zeta$ (33), and so the neighbours' $\dot w^{[j]}$ as well as their $w^{[j]}$:
each aircraft sends two numbers per parameter. Theorem 3: if the field's horizontal part never vanishes and
$\sigma(0) \neq \pi$, and if, during saturation, $\sigma$ stays on the side that the saturation corrects (its
Condition 2), then $\sigma \to 0$. Corollary 1 drops Condition 2: if $|\dot\theta_d| \le d < \min(-a, b)$, any
$k_\theta < \bar k_\theta = \min(-a - d,\ b - d)$ avoids saturation altogether.

What Theorem 3 gives is the heading. It does not say that the team then coordinates: once the aircraft follow the
partially normalised field, robot $i$'s virtual coordinate runs at $v/\|\chi^{[i]}_p\|$ times the rate of Theorem 1,
and that factor differs between robots. On a path where $\|f'\|$ changes, two aircraft at the same speed and a fixed
$\Delta \neq 0$ are at places where the path runs at different speeds, and they cannot both stay on it and keep the
spacing. With $\Delta^{[1,2]} = \pi/2$ on the curve of the first flight (everything else as flown), the coordination
error in the curve's parameter $\beta w$ still reaches `{python} f2(late(FL1d[0], 600)[:, 6].max())` rad in the second
half of a 20-minute flight, and the path error `{python} f1(late(FL1d[0], 600)[:, 1].max())` m: the aircraft trade
one against the other at every lap **[numerical]**. With $\Delta = 0$, as in both flights, the issue does not arise.

On the paper's first flight, run below in simulation, the largest $|\dot\theta_d|$ once the aircraft are on the
path is `{python} f3(d_thd)` rad/s. With a turn-rate limit of $0.8$ rad/s (assumed; the paper does not give one),
Corollary 1 then allows any $k_\theta$ below `{python} f2(0.8 - d_thd)`. The paper flies $k_\theta = 1$, above it, so
Corollary 1 does not apply and Theorem 3 needs its Condition 2. The corollary is sufficient, not necessary: in the
simulated flight the turn rate saturates in `{python} f1(100 * sat_all)` % of the one-second records, all of them
while the aircraft turn onto the path, and in `{python} f1(100 * sat_late)` % after 300 s **[numerical]**.


# The program each robot runs

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Before take-off, robot $i$ knows:** its path or surface $f^{[i]}$ and its derivatives; its gains $k_j$, $k_c$; its
neighbours $\mathcal N_i$ and the desired differences $\Delta^{[i,j]}$ with each of them; on a surface, the desired
parametric speeds $\dot w^*$.

**It keeps:** its virtual coordinates $w^{[i]}$ (one per parameter), which start anywhere.

**At every tick:** measure its position $x^{[i]}$; receive $w^{[j]}$ from each neighbour; compute
$\phi = x^{[i]} - f^{[i]}(w^{[i]})$, $c^{[i]} = -\sum_j (w^{[i]} - w^{[j]} - \Delta^{[i,j]})$ and the field
$\chi^{[i]}$; move with the first $n$ entries; advance $w^{[i]}$ with the last ones; send $w^{[i]}$ to the
neighbours. An aircraft also sends $\dot w^{[i]}$, and turns with (31).
:::

In Python, for a path, the whole on-board program is one function. The simulator calls `team_field`, which computes
the same thing for every robot:

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def program(x, w, f, df, w_nbrs, deltas, k, kc):
    """Robot i on a path: its position x (n numbers), its virtual coordinate w, its path f and f',
    what its neighbours sent (w_j) and the desired differences Delta^[i,j]. Returns its velocity and w_dot."""
    n = len(x)
    sg = 1.0 if n % 2 == 0 else -1.0
    fx, dfx = f(w), df(w)
    phi = [x[j] - fx[j] for j in range(n)]
    c = -sum((w - wj) - d for wj, d in zip(w_nbrs, deltas))
    u = [sg * dfx[j] - k[j] * phi[j] for j in range(n)]
    w_dot = sg + sum(k[j] * phi[j] * dfx[j] for j in range(n)) + kc * c
    return u, w_dot
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# the 21 programs against the stacked field of the simulator, at the start of the example
X = X21
gap_prog = 0.0
chis, _ = team_field(T21, X)
for i in range(N21):
    S = T21["S"][i]
    fn = lambda w, S=S: shape_eval(S, [w])[0]
    dfn = lambda w, S=S: shape_eval(S, [w])[1][0]
    nb = T21["N"][i]
    u, wd = program(X[i][:2], X[i][2], fn, dfn, [X[j][2] for j in nb],
                    [T21["ws_ref"][i][0] - T21["ws_ref"][j][0] for j in nb], T21["kg"][i], T21["kc"][0])
    gap_prog = max(gap_prog, max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(u + [wd], chis[i])))
```

At the example's start, the 21 programs and the simulator's field differ by `{python} e1(gap_prog)`.

# The simulator

The world, not the robots: Euler ticks with the commands held for one tick. For a single integrator a held command
is exact physics; the path error then settles at a small floor set by the tick, which halves when the tick halves.
The aircraft use the same ticks for (28). The box below holds the complete core of this page (click to open it).

end at $\dot w^*$.

```{python}

def coverage(run, robots, m=10):
    seen = set()
    for X in run:
        for i in robots:
            x = X[i]
            cell = tuple(min(m - 1, max(0, int((x[l] - T3l["S"][0]["m"][l] + 1) / 2 * m))) for l in range(3))
            seen.add(cell)
    return len(seen) / m ** 3
cov3 = coverage(run3l, [0, 1, 2]); cov1 = coverage(run3l, [0])
```

`{python} len(REF)` points on a cycle graph that follows the strokes (drawn three times narrower in $w_2$, since the
torus is three times wider around its axis than around its tube). After 20 s the largest surface error is
`{python} e1(err4[-1, 0])` and the largest coordination error `{python} e1(err4[-1, 1])`. Since all robots run at
the same $\dot w^*$, the pattern keeps its shape in the parameters and travels around the torus, around the tube and
around the axis at once.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The paper's Fig. 6, with a pattern of our own: the robots on the torus at t = 0, 6 and 20 s (blue), and their tracks (light)."
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(11, 3.8))
u, vv = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 48), np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 24))
for k, tt in enumerate((0.0, 6.0, 20.0)):
    kk = int(round(tt / 0.1))
    ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 3, k + 1, projection="3d")
    ax.plot_wireframe((2 + np.cos(vv)) * np.cos(u), (2 + np.cos(vv)) * np.sin(u), np.sin(vv), color=GREY, lw=0.25, alpha=0.4)
    if kk > 0:
        for i in range(len(REF)):
            P = np.array([X[i][:3] for X in run4[max(0, kk - 20): kk + 1]])
            ax.plot(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], P[:, 2], color=SOFT, lw=0.7)
    E = np.array([X[:3] for X in run4[kk]])
    ax.scatter(E[:, 0], E[:, 1], E[:, 2], color=BLUE, s=9, depthshade=False)
    ax.set_box_aspect((3, 3, 1)); ax.set_axis_off(); ax.view_init(elev=35, azim=-20 - 25 * k)
    ax.set_title(f"t = {tt:g} s")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## The two flights, in simulation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The two flights, in simulation: the distance to the path (left) and the coordination error (right). Dark: the Lissajous curve (Figs. 7 and 8 of the paper); light: the torus (Figs. 10 and 11). The aircraft start 380 m and 140 m apart."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for R, col, lbl in ((FL1[0], BLUE, "Lissajous"), (FL2[0], SOFT, "torus")):
    a1.semilogy(R[:, 0], np.maximum(R[:, 1], 1e-3), color=col, lw=1.4, label=lbl)
    a2.semilogy(R[:, 0], np.maximum(R[:, 6], 1e-8), color=col, lw=1.4, label=lbl)
a1.set_xlabel("t [s]"); a1.set_ylabel("largest path error [m]"); a1.legend(frameon=False); a1.grid(alpha=0.3)
a2.set_xlabel("t [s]"); a2.set_ylabel("coordination error (in β w) [rad]"); a2.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The flights use the scaled field that the paper states for them, $\phi_j = L\,(x_j - f_j(\beta w))$ with $L = 0.1$
(and $\beta = 0.01$ on the Lissajous curve, $\beta_1 = 0.005$ and $\beta_2 = 0.01$ on the torus). Up to a positive
factor, which the partial normalisation removes, this is the field (3) for the path $f(\beta w)$ with the gains $k/L$
and $k_c\,\beta/L^3$ (one line of algebra, ours), and that is how the page flies it, with an airspeed of 12 m/s and a
turn-rate limit of 0.8 rad/s (neither is in the paper). The simulated aircraft converge in a few minutes and then fly about one metre apart, the GPS bias, with path errors
below `{python} f1(late(FL1[0], 300)[:, 1].max())` m on the Lissajous curve. The real flights also had wind (10 km/h)
and an autopilot whose airspeed changes when it climbs; the paper reports errors of one to two metres. The page does
not model the autopilot.

# What changes with more robots, and what this page does not cover

**More robots.** Nothing in the field depends on $N$: each robot computes its own $\chi^{[i]}$ from its own path and
its neighbours' $w$, and the communication per robot depends on its number of neighbours only (two on a cycle,
whatever $N$). Theorem 1 holds for any $N$ **[proved]**. What changes is the speed: the slowest mode of the
coordination has the graph's $\lambda_2$, which on a cycle falls as $4\pi^2/N^2$, and @sec-rate divides it further
by $\|f'\|^2$ **[numerical]**, for the circle's linearisation.

**Not covered here.**

- Time-varying $\Delta^{[i,j]}(t)$ and time-varying paths: the paper leaves them to future work.
- Switching graphs: the paper's conclusion points to consensus results for them; the page does not simulate them.
- The safety certificate's deadlocks (the paper's remark, Wang et al. Section VII): the page shows robots that dodge,
  not robots that block each other.
- The aircraft's low-level loops (bank and climb), and the wind in the flights. The figure of @sec-air has a wind
  slider, which the program does not know about **[numerical]**.
- A coordination in Euclidean distance rather than in the parameter: the paper names it as future work.

# Glossary

$f^{[i]}$
: robot $i$'s path $f^{[i]}(w)$ or surface $f^{[i]}(w_1, w_2)$, in $\mathbb R^n$.

$w^{[i]}$, $\xi^{[i]}$
: robot $i$'s virtual coordinate(s), and its generalised coordinate $(x^{[i]}, w^{[i]})$.

$\phi^{[i]}_j$, $\Phi$
: the path (or surface) errors $x_j - f_j(w)$, and all of them stacked.

$\chi^{[i]}$
: robot $i$'s coordinating guiding vector field, (5) or (17).

$c^{[i]}$, $k_c$
: the coordination function (7), and its gain.

$\Delta^{[i,j]}$, $w^*$
: the desired parametric difference on the edge $(i, j)$, and a reference with $\Delta^{[i,j]} = w^{[i]*} - w^{[j]*}$.

$L$, $D$, $\lambda_2$
: the Laplacian and an incidence matrix of the graph, $L = DD^\top$, and its smallest nonzero eigenvalue.

$V$
: the Lyapunov function of the proofs, (41) and (55).

$v$, $\dot w^*$
: the extra vector of the surface field (14), and the desired parametric speeds of Theorem 2.

$R$, $\alpha$, $\mathcal D_i$
: the safety distance, the gain of the barrier, and the robots robot $i$ keeps away from in (QP2).

$v$ (aircraft), $\theta$, $\sigma$
: the airspeed, the course, and the angle from the field's horizontal direction to the course.

$\dot\theta_d$, $k_\theta$, $a$, $b$
: the turn rate of the field's direction (32), the heading gain, and the saturation limits of (31).
